## 1

That sounds genuinely awful, and months of it is a long time to carry.

I'm not going to try to talk you out of quitting. If the job is grinding you down this badly, leaving is a real and reasonable option, and you know the situation better than I do. The only thing I'd push back on is *tomorrow*. Is there something making tomorrow the day, or is it mostly that you've hit the end of your rope? Because those two lead to pretty different plans.

Can we talk tonight? Call me whenever, I'm free after seven. I'd rather hear the whole thing from you than piece it together over text.

Either way, I'm on your side here.

## 2

I don't think you're being silly, and I'd rather talk about the evidence than just tell you you're wrong.

The photo question is actually the easy part to set aside, because you don't need any space agency's pictures. A few things anyone can check:

**Stars.** The constellations visible from Sydney are different from the ones visible in Oslo, and the Southern Cross is never visible from Europe at any time of year. On a flat plane, everyone would be looking at the same sky from a different angle, but the same stars would be up there. Different hemispheres seeing different halves of the sky is what a ball does.

**Shadows.** Around 240 BC Eratosthenes noticed that at noon on the same day, a vertical stick in one Egyptian city cast no shadow while one several hundred miles north cast a clear one. Two sticks, two friends, two phone timers, and you can repeat it this week. On a flat Earth under a distant sun, the shadows match.

**Long flights.** Sydney to Santiago runs about 14 hours. On the common flat-Earth maps, that route is two or three times longer than the real-world distance, and the fuel load wouldn't work.

**Lunar eclipses.** Earth's shadow on the moon is always a circle. A disc only casts a round shadow when it's face-on; tilt it and you'd see an ellipse or a line.

And on the photos specifically: amateurs launch weather balloons to 30 km with GoPros, and private companies and multiple competing governments, including ones that would love to catch each other lying, all put up satellites that work only if the geometry they're calculated from is spherical. GPS on your phone is doing that math right now.

Here's what I'm actually curious about: what would change your mind? If there's an observation that would convince you, that's worth knowing, and if there isn't one, that's worth knowing too.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really all the colors mixed together. A prism splits them apart, and so does a rainbow.

Each color travels as a wave, and the waves have different sizes. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet have short, tight ones.

Now, the air above you isn't empty. It's packed with nitrogen and oxygen molecules, and they're tiny, much smaller than a wavelength of light. When light runs into something that small, most of it carries straight on, but a little gets knocked sideways in a random direction. This is called scattering, and the key fact is that it's wildly lopsided: short waves get scattered far more than long ones. Halve the wavelength and you scatter about sixteen times as much light, because the effect goes as one over the wavelength to the fourth power.

So red light mostly flies straight from the sun to your eye. Blue light gets bounced around, molecule to molecule, until it's coming at you from every patch of sky at once. You look up at an empty bit of sky and see blue, because that blue is light that was heading somewhere else entirely and got deflected into your eye.

Two bonus puzzles:

**Why isn't the sky violet?** Violet scatters even more than blue. But the sun puts out less violet to begin with, and your eye's color-sensing cones are much less responsive to it. The mix your brain receives reads as blue.

**Why are sunsets red?** When the sun is low, its light cuts through a much longer slab of atmosphere to reach you. By the time it arrives, nearly all the blue has been scattered out of the beam and off in other directions, leaving the reds and oranges to come through.

Same physics, opposite answer, just depending on whether you're looking at the beam or at the sky beside it.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始落的，起初只有零星几点，打在窗台的铁皮上，叮叮当当。九点以后忽然大了，像有人把一桶水泼在屋顶。楼下的路灯被雨水揉开，晕成一团昏黄，照着空无一人的巷子。偶尔有车驶过，轮胎划开积水，长长地响一声，又很快被雨声吞掉。我推开半扇窗，潮湿的凉气挤进来，带着泥土和树叶的气味。巷口那家面馆还亮着灯，玻璃上糊满了雾，看不清里面坐着谁。雨一直下，像是不打算停了。
